narration.text: This drone has no pilot.
Many times a second it measures its height and decides how hard to spin its propellers.
Watch the gust push it down. It climbs back on its own.
In this lesson you'll build that decision yourself.
Suppose the drone is below its target. What should it do?
Got it. Here's how the drone decides.
Too low means more thrust, so it climbs. Too high means less, so it sinks.

feedback.correct: Yes: too low means push harder.
feedback.incorrect: Pushing less would let it sink further. Too low needs more thrust, so it climbs.
feedback.unsure: That's a fair place to start. Too low needs more thrust, so it climbs.

narration.text: Measure: the height sensor under the body reads how high the drone is.
Compare: the gap between where it is and where it should be is called the error.
Correct: it changes its thrust to close the gap, then measures again.
Every controller in this lesson only ever looks at that gap. The question is how to turn a gap into thrust.

explanation.title: The feedback loop
explanation.body: Measure the height, compare it with the target, correct the thrust, and repeat. The error is the target height minus the measured height.
assumptions: the drone moves only up and down
drag is simplified and exaggerated so the bounce dies out quickly

narration.text: Here's the simplest rule: push harder the bigger the gap. That's P, for proportional.
Where will the drone end up?
Got it. Press Run to test your guess.
It rises, bobs, and settles below the line, short by {{final_error_m}}.
At rest the thrust arrow and the weight arrow are the same length.

feedback.correct: You predicted below the target, and that is what happened.
feedback.incorrect: You expected it somewhere else. It settles below the target, and here is why.
feedback.unsure: You weren't sure, and that's fine. It settles below the target, and here is why.

narration.text: To hover, thrust must equal the drone's weight.
But P only pushes when there's a gap.
So the drone sinks until the gap is just big enough to make that thrust. No gap, no push.

explanation.title: Why P alone hovers low
explanation.body: At rest the speed is zero, so the only push is P: Kp times the gap. To hold the drone up that push must equal its weight, so a gap has to remain. A bigger Kp needs a smaller gap, but never none.
assumptions: the drone moves only up and down
drag is simplified and exaggerated so the bounce dies out quickly
limits: a basic PID does not know the drone's weight; it only sees the gap

narration.text: Think of cruise control on a hill.
The hill pulls the car back, the way gravity pulls the drone down.
With a P-like rule the car settles a little slower than the set speed, just as the drone settles a little low.
A driver who notices the car has been slow for a while keeps pressing a little more, and closes the gap. That's I, which you'll try on the drone soon.
Now the car becomes the drone: the set speed is the target height, the hill is gravity, and the accelerator is the thrust.
Where it breaks down: a car controls speed, but the drone controls height, one more step between push and result.
That step is why the drone bounces and this car doesn't, so the car has no bounce for D to fix. D belongs to the drone.
And a driver sees the hill coming; a basic PID only reacts to the gap it already has.
Let's try a much bigger P. The first run stays on the plot as a faint ghost line.
Press Run when you're ready.
The gap shrinks to {{final_error_m}}.
But the drone now shoots higher past where it ends up, by {{overshoot_m}}, and this time it crosses the target line before settling back below it.
So why not just make P huge?

choices.label: It trades the gap for bounce

feedback.correct: Right: a smaller gap, but more bounce.
feedback.incorrect: Bigger is not always better: the gap shrinks, but the bounce grows.
feedback.unsure: Here's the catch: the gap shrinks, but the bounce grows.

narration.text: More P means harder pushes, so the drone shoots further past.
And the motors have a maximum: push hard enough and they run out.
Let's fix the bounce first.
If you were flying it by hand, what would you do as it rushes up toward the line?
Got it. Here's the rule that does that.
D, for derivative, watches how fast the drone is moving and pushes against that speed.
Rushing up means it eases off before it overshoots.

feedback.correct: Yes: easing off early is exactly the idea.
feedback.incorrect: Pushing harder would make it shoot further past. The fix is to ease off early.
feedback.unsure: That's fine. The fix is to ease off early, as it rushes up.

narration.text: The three bars beside the drone show what P, I and D each add to the thrust.
Press Run and watch the D bar point down while the drone climbs.
The bounce is gone. The gap is still there: {{final_error_m}}.
Notice D didn't fix the gap. At rest the speed is zero, so D adds nothing.
The drone has been too low for a while now. What kind of rule would notice that?
Got it. Here's the rule that remembers.
I, for integral, keeps a running total of the gap over time.
While the drone stays low, the total keeps growing and adds more thrust, until the gap is closed.

feedback.correct: Yes: a rule that remembers how long the gap has lasted.
feedback.incorrect: A stronger P or D still sees only the gap now, or the speed now. To notice 'too low for a while' the rule has to remember.
feedback.unsure: That's fine. To notice 'too low for a while' the rule has to remember the gap.

narration.text: Now all three together. Press Run.
It reaches the line, and the gap closes.
Look at the bars at rest: P and D are back to nothing, and the I bar alone holds up the weight.
Now the memory is doing the holding, so the gap can be zero.
Now pick the Too much I preset and press Run.
It shoots past and rings, and the checks strip warns that it is still oscillating.
I has momentum. Its total takes time to unwind, so it keeps pushing after the drone has passed the line.
Tuning is a balance.
We bolt on a camera, so the drone is heavier.
With P and D only, will the gap be bigger, smaller or the same?
Got it. Press Run to test your guess.
The gap grows to {{final_error_m}}.
More weight needs more thrust, and P only makes thrust from a gap, so it needs a bigger gap.

feedback.correct: You predicted a bigger gap, and that is what happened.
feedback.incorrect: You expected otherwise. The gap grows, and here is why.
feedback.unsure: You weren't sure, and that's fine. The gap grows, and here is why.

narration.text: A steady wind pushes down. Which term brings the drone back to exactly the target?

feedback.incorrect: Not that one. P needs a gap to push, and D needs speed, so neither can hold the drone exactly on target against a steady push.

narration.text: Watch: the wind starts and pushes the drone down.
I keeps adding while the drone is low, until it holds the weight and the wind together, with no gap left.
Tell me in one sentence each what P, I and D do. Say it to yourself, then compare.
Compare your sentences with these. This is a self-check, not a grade.
P pushes in proportion to the gap now. D pushes against the speed, which damps the bounce.
I adds up the gap over time, so at rest it holds the weight with no gap left.

explanation.title: Key points to compare with
explanation.body: A feedback controller measures, compares with the target and corrects, over and over. P pushes in proportion to the current gap. With gravity, P alone leaves the drone below the target, because it needs a gap to make the thrust that holds it up. D pushes against the speed of change, which damps the bounce; at rest it adds nothing. I adds up the gap over time, so it keeps increasing thrust until the gap is zero; at rest it holds the weight. Too much P or I causes overshoot and ringing; too much D makes it sluggish.
limits: a self-check in prepared mode; Aili grades a typed answer only in live mode

narration.text: Where this model stops: real drones also tilt and move sideways; this one only goes up and down.
Real motors take time to speed up, real height sensors are noisy, and the drag here is exaggerated.
The numbers teach the idea. They are not settings for tuning a real drone.

explanation.title: Where the model stops
explanation.body: This is a simplified teaching model.
assumptions: the drone moves only up and down
drag is simplified and exaggerated so the bounce dies out quickly
limits: real drones also tilt and move sideways
real motors take time to speed up; here thrust changes instantly
real height sensors are noisy, and D amplifies noise, so real controllers filter it
real flight controllers usually add a hover-thrust estimate and run several loops inside each other
the numbers teach the idea; they are not settings for tuning a real drone

narration.text: You just tuned a controller by hand, the way engineers do.
Some robots now learn their controllers through practice. That's a later lesson.
